title: Blonde (2022) didn’t quite receive the accolades it deserved

commenti.body: It’s truly baffling to me that your take isn’t the consensus. That year it seemed the films that deserved to be praised ended up on the back burner or were too divisive to receive the universal acclaim they really deserved. Blonde and Babylon to me really stood out with Tar not far behind. It’s so regrettable that a piece of fluff like “Everything….” Took home every Oscar under the sun when films like this were largely forgotten or ignored. I feel the same way about Saltburn.

>...depict various stages in the troubled life of one of the Golden Age’s most troubled icons.

​

>"I think Blonde is a work of fiction and it's got just as much Joyce \[Carol Oates\] in it as it does Marilyn."  
Andrew Dominik

So there's a problem right for starters, an epistemological one about what do we know about Marylin as opposed to what we see in the film. Is it a historical-biographical study as you suggest or a completely or mostly fictional piece?

Because the boundaries are blurred, with documentary-style recreations of her iconic film sequences and photos, the film looks like a standard biopic. Ana de Armas' performance is good but is too "fake Marylin" to be convincing as a real person rather than as a media icon. 

Then there's the question of agency - Marylin appears to be more or less powerless, victim of cinema moguls and abusive or cold husbands. Biographical evidence seems to suggest otherwise, that she had quite some considerable degree of control over her career and love life. She's too much the victim, in other words. 

So it would have been much better as a much more fictionalised and less apparently "realistic" docu-style depiction. A more iconic approach which distanced the film from the reality overtly, would have helped it immensely IMO.

I've been thinking about watching this film since it came out, but all of the discourse surrounding it has given me pause. Some critics called it sexist, Joyce Carol Oates called it "utterly feminist", it got an NC17 rating supposedly for graphic SA, etc etc. The Wikipedia page is basically an absolute roller coaster.

Obviously I should just watch it & form my own opinions, but it's hard not to be nervous after everything I've read (also because I absolutely adore Assassination of Jesse James and I don't want my opinion of Dominik to be tarnished)

How did you feel about the critical response surrounding this film? Was it unfair?

I disagree that the movie looked docu-style. There's a very dreamy/nightmarish undercurrent throughout the whole movie with really strange visual choices, and several outright surreal sequences, like Terrence Malick combined with David Lynch. Only the black-and-white scenes felt "grounded" imo. The marketing portrayed this as a traditional biopic for obvious reasons, but I think it's clear from watching the first ten minutes that it's not.

The problem is that the movie's concept is just a nonstarter. Just an inherently offensive and controversial premise from the beginning. I'm sure Joyce Carol Oates's book is quite good but that has the benefit of being text that can more easily remove itself from the backlash of portraying an iconic and celebrated figure in such a nasty way.

And I think the backlash to this movie is pretty warranted lol. It’s hilariously hateful, and even attempts to warp the legacy of some of Marilyn's old movies by interspersing re-enactments of her classic scenes with shots of FICTIONAL trauma to undermine her acting abilities. It’s absolutely wild, but I will admit I had a great time watching it because of how offensive it is while simultaneously showcasing really impressive filmmaking. But it's definitely a weird-ass movie and not at all a surprise that people hate it.

I'm sorry but Blonde was terrible IMO. I honestly couldn't even make it halfway through. It felt like it was trying way too hard to be something else, and that made me and my wife lose interest midway through.
That’s because it was something else

We could zoom in on a pair of sequences, I think they're next to each other in the film, but I can't remember right now and don't feel like checking.

The one sequence recreates the famous "upskirt" shot from ***The 7 Year Itch***. It is an exact recreation, so much so that not many people could differentiate between the original and this remake. The style of film, the mise-en-scene, everything is painstakingly recreated. This is what I mean by the docu-style.

Then there's the premiere of the same film (I think). The atmosphere now is pure horror, music and framing make it hugely unsettling. This is the Lynchian atmosphere you refer to. If the film was all like this, and particularly if it had avoided direct reference to MM as a historical personality, I think it would have worked as a borderline horror portrait of star celebrity. 

Minus the crappy snorricam of course. 

Even the "communing with my foetus" and "doctors forced me to do it" bits could have kinda worked in this context. It's when it is cloaked in biopic disguise that the confusion reigns. 

Now myth becomes fact, precisely the creepy effect that the movie is ostensibly railing against.

Didn't quite receive accolades is a pretty big understatement. Lots of people really go out of their way to hate it.

It gets painted as a real hit piece on Marilyn. That its cruel and one sided and exploitative and over the top obnoxious.  And while I don't think it's a ton of fun to watch, I understand the approach and attitude it's trying to convey by purposely showing only the worst possible scenario and events for Marilyn as a contrast to the glitz and glamor it assumes you already know and have seen about her.  

It beats you down with just pure degradation of her, because yeah. Those are all things, across her and her life's timeline, that compounded on her and wore her down too. It's not glamorizing or condoning how any of this is great or that she's weak or how you, at home, will suffer the same fate. It's just trying to elicit some empathy for a personality that has been portrayed mostly as airheaded, tawdry, or a pushover for years before being adopted as a sex symbol to emulate and aspire to be.  

You shouldn't like it's tone. You shouldn't like what happens to her. But a ton of the outrage for this has come back at the filmmakers. But as we go forward tons and tons more debaucherous shit bubbles to the surface about stars you know. What about stars you don't?  Do you really think human behavior just snapped at the onset of social media and everyone was pristine little angels who played nice before it?  Bad things happened. To a lot of people.  To a lot of women. And I guess a lot of people don't want to hear about it because it's uncomfortable.  But her bad life should have light shed on it. As a warning and message that there sometimes is a lot of pain and damage hidden behind a smile and that the cost of glamor and fame was once very high.

Oh gotcha, in that context I agree - especially your last sentence. The movie's very exploitative specifically because of what you brought up.

And I also thought the snorricam shots were out of place and terrible looking haha. So many bizarre choices in this movie, like Andrew Dominik just wanted to experiment with weird techniques and film Ana de Armas naked as much as possible

Honestly, OP, I couldn’t agree less. After the scene where her unborn fetus chastises her for getting an abortion, not long after we watch an offscreen President force her to suck his dick while she does voice-over about it, I don’t think I could have been more repulsed. The rest of the film certainly did not help.  
  
Honestly my least favorite movie of the last few years. It was just repulsive.

And a lot of those scenes were based on gross rumors, it felt like an exploitative fantasy than a true examination of her life and persona. It’s a good looking film but the subject matter was handled poorly. The director himself has careless [attitude](https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/interviews/im-not-interested-reality-im-interested-images-andrew-dominik-blonde) on her filmography and accomplishments. I don’t see nostalgia in this film at all.
It’s a lot like Stone’s JFK. A big exercise is American myth making, playing fast and loose with facts in order to leave you with an emotional truth. I loved it.

A lot of her fans do know about the scandalous parts of her personal life. What I have seen people take issue with is it incorporates things that are just rumor or never happened. Most of the biopics that get made about her are about 'Revealing what is behind the curtain.' If you make something featuring her and her persona then that aspect is pretty much expected as a storytelling feature. The book and movie are pieces of biographical fiction but I think if you say 'We are making something about her pain and how she was exploited.' Then people will respond on those terms.

There’s nothing abt the film to suggest that realism was the goal. As OP points out, Dominick does all he can to show you it’s not realistic. 

There are serious problems with the film, but a lack of realism - when nothing abt the movie suggest realism is being depicted - isn’t one of them.

So the original 7 Year Itch promo was a staged media event - it was a ‘re-presentation’ of a manufactured reality. 

Which is exactly what the rest of the film is. 

The point is, we *think* the media gives us information about celebrities, but nothing you see in the media can be trusted more than any work of fiction. It’s all staged.
This echos Jesse James by the way, which is suffused with commentary on the inaccuracies of celebrity myth

It is explicitly an adaptation of a work of biographical fiction, so this confusion you are citing is not real. It never at any point claimed to be a documentary or an accurate reflection of the real person named Marilyn Monroe, and I genuinely consider criticisms coming at it from that angle to be unfair and illegitimate to a large extent. It does not deserve to be saddled with responsibility it did not ask for. People are allowed to play around with the mythic figures that have emerged in the cultural consciousness.

I hear you. And it does paint the darkest possible timeline for her: assuming that every rumor was true and boiling down complex relationships and dealings into just pure evil. But I think there was an overarching story being told here, beyond Marilyn Monroe. It's why it and the book are called Blonde, not Marilyn. She's just the unfortunate poster child for scandalous abuse, manipulation, degradation...dehumanization. Dished out to more blondes throughout Hollywood history than we could count. 

It's big weakness and failure to me is a marketing one. Because you're right: people would have responded better to this if it was promoted in some kind of context. But it wasn't. It made headlines as "shocking Marilyn Monroe movie" and got shoved through the ringer and labeled all the stuff it's been, stripping it's message away underneath a ton of other side quibbles about it. Like the authenticity or the graphic nature being zeroed in on. 

May December is a more recent, and more balanced, approach with the same core idea of: how does tragedy and manipulation effect someone. And in May December's case they were wise enough to distance the characters enough to tell the story they wanted to tell, not the specific one that happened.

I genuinely would like to see more deeper dives and analysis done on this one. I think it's one of the few films whose cruelty and darkness serve a purpose and has been interpreted the wrong way by a lot of folks.

As much as I would like to be a contrarian, championing this film as an overly derided victim of adjacent cultural discourse…. it just isn’t… which pains me to say because Dominik’s previous work The Assassination of Jesse James is one of my favorite films of all time. I enjoy miserable, depressing films. I love Bela Tarr, Michael Haneke, et al- filmmakers often mislabeled as misanthropes imo- but Blonde felt to me like a genuinely misanthropic, spiteful work which does not care for the humanity of any of its characters. I get what the film is doing, it’s violently tearing down a traditional American cultural monument, examining the dark underpinnings of a larger story we like to tell ourselves. This isn’t new, ‘Jesse James’, and to a lesser extent Killing Them Softly also did it. But while those films upended American tropes of exceptionalism, fortitude, and individualism by examining their characters with empathy, nuance, and a surprising amount of grace, Blonde takes every opportunity to not go more than skin deep into the fictional Marylyn’s psyche, and instead revels in cheap, surface level humiliation tactics and torturous scenery chewing for most of its runtime. It’s a really tiring, disappointing film, and I’m not excited for the inevitable cultural reappraisal it’s going to receive in 10-20 years.

I refer you to the OP's comment that it "depict\[s\] various stages in the troubled life of one of the Golden Age’s most troubled iconTheTh

The confusion is very much there, however much we self-described media sophisticates may fool ourselves into imagining it's not.

I wasn’t confused at all, and I don’t think anyone involved in the making of the film was confused, so I’m not sure why criticism has to account for people failing to grasp the (to me) obvious intent. I truly think that there is nothing the film could have done, while still being a fictional biography of Marilyn Monroe, that would have protected it from being misunderstood by some people. It’s just the nature of the beast and thus imo cannot be held against it.

This is such a gross oversimplification of what happens in the film. You're looking at these things through a political context that just isn't there. The fetus, the president stuff, it's just not some wholly cruel exercise you're making it out to be. Seeing these conservative comments makes me concerned as to whether or not you even watched the movie. 

Like your viewing it through a lens of how we're living in a time where it's important to present women as empowered, and you want to reinvent Marilyn Monroe as an empowered woman. Aside from the fact that it's a film. A work of fiction. A character. Much like Monroe was, as opposed to Norma Jean. IMO obviously. Just strange and limiting to watch things like this.

There you have it! I actually would prefer that writers and filmmakers do avoid fictionalized biographies, certainly those that clearly identify a fictional character with a historical person. 

Though I would never suggest banning them or anything like that, I just think there is indeed something fraught about the whole business. 

It's all very well to say we don't have to account for people's misunderstandings about biographical facts, but how many people went away thinking Norma Jean got nearly drowned and was permanently traumatized by her mother's abuse? 

When the Wiki on her states "Monroe's early childhood was stable and happy" (I'm not an expert on her life story so I don't have better sources than that.) 

There are so many issues with how her life story is framed and there is IMO no clear indication to the viewing public that this is fictionalized. 

Finally it represents exploitation of a dead person's memory, whatever the intent may be. Jesse James never got that treatment.

Joyce Carol Oates wrote the novel it is based on, so she's not very unbiased. This is one that, if you don't have a critic you really trust and are often on the same wavelength with, I don't know how you are really going to come to any conclusions without watching it yourself. The reactions are all over the place, literally from masterpiece to the worst piece of shit you've ever seen. I'm a big defender, personally, but I'm just some random schmuck so that won't help you much.
This is a bit defensive and assumes a lot about how I viewed the movie and what I thought about it lol

Yeah, that's a position I can easily respect for its consistency and the obvious basic respect for human dignity that is motivating it. I guess I have too much of an iconoclastic streak in me and admire the boldness of making a movie like Blonde.

The moments you've mentioned of the entire film add up to about 2 minutes of content. You aren't getting into structure or narrative, not even character beyond what you were hoping to see from a preconcieved notion. The argument reads like it was made in bad faith. Not to be meant as a diss, just what I thought when reading it.

I just find it interesting that there was already an adaptation of the novel in like 2002 that seemed well received. Most of my friends also seemed to think it was a proper Marilyn biopic based on her life. Not that it was adapted from a book, and a *fictional* book at that!
Your sexism will not be tolerated. I am a mod.

Absolutely no idea how there's anything sexist in my post? This quote? “Now we’re living in a time where it’s important to present women as empowered, and they want to reinvent Marilyn Monroe as an empowered woman. That’s what they want to see,” Dominik said. “And if you’re not showing them that, it upsets them.”

This x 1,000,000,000.

The flick is essentially misogynist torture porn - emphasis on the porn - masquerading as art.

Repulsive stuff.
Everything... was s*it I agree 👍 blonde is a much better film with all its shortcomings

I didn’t love it but I appreciated what they were trying to do. Theres so many rumors and conflicting accounts of her life idk how you would even make an accurate movie about her, it seems better to just lean in to the surrealism to me. 

Netflix and everyone involved really set themselves up for failure though, I don’t the reaction would have been nearly as bad if they fought the NC-17 rating and they didn’t have Ana claiming to be haunted by Marilyn or whatever that was.

Honestly the NC17 rating is very harsh for what it is. 

The abortion scene is probably the most graphic and even that didn’t seem worse than anything you’d see on any random true crime show to me. Idg why they didn’t fight it because a lot of more graphic stuff gets an R easily.
What did he say that was sexist??

In all honesty, even if you stripped away all the extremely gross, unnecessary, and problematic trash within the film, I would say that Blonde is basically a bloated piece of pretentious nonsense. There are glimpses, very small glimpses, of interesting cinematic ideas, but the ego of the filmmaker can be felt from second one throughout. The cinematography is at times pretty or striking and at other times it is nauseating or goofy. I also think that Ana de Armas' performance isn't good. I'm sorry, it's nothing against her, but I found it hammy and void. This could be due to direction or writing or maybe just some creative mistakes made somewhere along the line.

Personally, I am glad a film like Blonde flopped, because I think 10 years ago, it would've been a hit or at least much more well liked. Im happy that the general movie going population kind of seems to want to shift away from this miserable, self-indulgent, nihilistic Filmmaking that I feel really has saturated the landscape of cinema for the past 10ish years.
